name: Thiripuranthakeswarar Temple, Koovam
deity: Shiva as Thiripuranthakeswarar (Thripuranthakar), the self-manifested linga, with the goddess Thiripurasundari
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Thondai country, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); structural temple with medieval and later additions
summary: Thiripuranthakeswarar is the Shiva temple of Tiruvirkolam on the banks of the Koovam river, a Paadal Petra Sthalam of the Thondai country sung by Tirugnanasambandar, where the Lord is worshipped as Tripurantaka, the destroyer of the three cities, who is said to have revealed himself here bearing the bow.

sections.history: Koovam, on the river that shares its name in the Thondai country north-west of Chennai, is an old temple village whose shrine is praised in the Tevaram. In the hymns the place is called Tiruvirkolam, and because it is counted among the Thondai Nadu temples sung by the saints it is honoured as a Paadal Petra Sthalam; the child-saint Tirugnanasambandar is remembered as having sung its decad. The name Tiruvirkolam is read as the sacred form bearing the bow, for the Lord is worshipped here as Tripurantaka, who took up the bow to end the three flying cities of the asuras. The linga of the sanctum is held to be swayambhu, self-manifested rather than set in place by human hands. The great tank beside the temple carries a memory reaching back to the Chola age, and the shrine has been kept in worship across the centuries, raised and enlarged in stone by the patrons of the Tamil country.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered from the south through a five-tiered rajagopuram, and the sanctum is crowned by a Gajaprishta vimana, the apsidal tower shaped like the back of a resting elephant. Within, the linga of Thiripuranthakeswarar is revered as a self-manifested stone that the priests do not touch with their hands, from which the Lord carries the name Theenda Tirumeni Nathar, the Lord of the form not to be touched. The goddess Thiripurasundari is honoured in her own shrine, and devotees are traditionally bidden to pray to her before approaching the Lord. Beside the temple lies the Agni Theertham, a tank that tradition says has never run dry even in years of famine, and the Koovam river itself is said to take its rise near this sacred spot.
sections.legends: The temple keeps the great legend of Tripura. The three cities of the asuras, raised of gold, silver and iron, flew through the three worlds and could be destroyed only when they came into a single line; Shiva made the earth his chariot, the sun and moon its wheels, and the mountain Meru his bow, and with a single arrow reduced the three cities to ash. At Tiruvirkolam the Lord is remembered as revealing that martial form, bow in hand, and from this the town takes its name, the sacred place of the form with the bow. The self-manifested linga, which no hand may touch, is honoured as a sign of a presence that was never fashioned but always was.
sections.festivals: The temple's principal festival is the ten-day Chithirai Brahmotsavam in April or May, when the Lord is drawn in procession through the village. Maha Shivaratri in February or March is kept with night-long worship, and the Arudra Darshan of Margazhi in December or January, sacred to the dancing Shiva, is observed with devotion, as is the monthly Pradosham. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Koovam rewards a quiet, unhurried visit far from the noise of the city. Enter through the southern gopuram, pause at the Agni Theertham, and offer prayers first to the goddess Thiripurasundari before coming to the Lord in the sanctum, as tradition asks. Couples seeking harmony in married life hold the place especially dear, and many devotees walk to the riverside, mindful that the Koovam is said to rise here. Set among fields in the Thondai country, the temple keeps the stillness of an old village sanctuary.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Koovam lies in Tiruvallur district, near Perambakkam and the Kadambattur road, roughly 50 to 70 km west of Chennai by different reckonings. The temple stands about a kilometre from the Koovam bus stop, and buses reach the village from Tiruvallur and the surrounding towns; Tiruvallur, on the Chennai suburban railway, is the convenient rail point. Confirm the route locally before setting out.
